chunks: BLDC from a microcontroller. The question: How do you control a BLDC motor from a microcontroller? What other components do you need?
A microcontroller (MCU) cannot drive a BLDC motor directly. Its pins give only milliamps, and the motor needs amps at 12 volts or more.
So you place a power stage between them: gate drivers and six MOSFET switches. The MCU sends small timing signals; the power stage does the heavy lifting.
Think of the power steering in a car. Your hands turn the wheel with little force, but the hydraulic booster does the real work of moving the heavy wheels.
The MCU is your hands, and the gate driver and MOSFETs are the booster.
The analogy has one gap: the MCU also listens for feedback, such as rotor position and current, to know what the motor actually did.
The signal chain. Six logic PWM lines leave the MCU, the driver converts them into proper gate waveforms, and the bridge drives the motor.
Hall, current and fault signals return to the MCU on the left and bottom pins.
MOSFET: a transistor (a part a small signal can turn on and off) used as a fast, powerful switch.
Half-bridge: two MOSFETs stacked between the supply and ground, with one motor phase (coil group) connected between them.
PWM: switching on and off very fast, so the fraction of on-time sets the average voltage. Gate driver: a chip that delivers the burst of current needed to switch MOSFETs fast.
Dead-time: a short pause so the two switches of a half-bridge are never both on. Shunt resistor: a tiny resistor used to measure current.
Say a motor draws 3 amps from a 12 volts supply, and an MCU pin can supply about 20 milliamps (a typical figure). The motor needs 3 / 0.
02 = 150 times more current than the pin can give.
The chain is: MCU makes six PWM signals, the gate driver boosts them, three half-bridges (six MOSFETs) switch the supply, and the motor turns.
Hall sensors and a current shunt report back to the MCU. That is the whole idea: the MCU commands, the power stage delivers.
"I can't drive a BLDC from GPIO.
I need a three-phase bridge of six N-MOSFETs, a gate driver to level-shift and supply gate current, and an MCU with complementary PWM and dead-time to command it.
Feedback comes from Hall sensors or back-EMF, a shunt plus amplifier for current, and a divider for bus voltage.
I'd add a hardware overcurrent trip into the timer's break input, a bulk DC-link capacitor, and local supplies.
Or I'd use an integrated BLDC driver and just supply PWM and Halls."
